strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in LLM-based software engineering. Its three-level workflow coherently integrates localization, repair, code analysis, retrieval, and testing, with a reasonable motivation for escalating effort after unsuccessful repairs.

The evaluation spans four benchmarks, three programming languages, and seven LLM backbones. The reported 197 correct Defects4J repairs, complete QuixBugs coverage, and consistent improvements over CoT prompting on ConDefects are promising evidence of practical utility.

The agent descriptions, workflow diagrams, system prompts, pseudocode, and source-code link help readers understand and potentially reproduce the approach. Distinguishing test-passing patches from semantically correct repairs is also appropriate.
weaknesses: The correctness evidence needs an audit. Appendix A.4 describes Figure 23 as a successful repair, but its boundary checks inspect the last hexadecimal digit. For the manuscript’s own input, 0x80000000, it selects createInteger and still throws NumberFormatException; I confirmed this with a small Java reproduction of the printed logic. The manual adjudication protocol underlying the 197 correct repairs is also unspecified. This example does not invalidate every aggregate result, but the contradiction requires validated patches, test logs, and explicit correctness criteria.

Important results are internally inconsistent: Table 1 reports 286 plausible UniDebugger repairs, whereas Tables 2 and 4 report 291; RewardRepair has 90 correct repairs but only 75 plausible repairs, contradicting the metric definitions. Historical baseline results also cover differing benchmark versions or subsets. Reconcile these counts and provide per-bug outcomes and comparisons on common evaluated bugs to substantiate the headline improvement.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed hierarchical coordination mechanism. Adding agents also increases model calls, available information, and tool access. A comparison with a single agent using equivalent tools and computational budget, together with a flat or always-L3 configuration, would distinguish the benefits of hierarchy from those of additional inference and context. The present evidence supports the combined pipeline more directly than the claimed superiority of its cognitive organization.

The cost-effectiveness claim uses incomparable sampling units. A UniDebugger attempt can involve several agents, multiple candidate patches, and refinements, whereas baseline sampling counts need not represent equivalent work. Table 2 reports expense per run rather than total expense per bug under the retry budget. Comparable total token usage, model calls, tool execution costs, and repair-versus-budget measurements are needed.

The end-to-end localization assumption remains underspecified. Algorithm 1 receives the already identified 'bug-located file' as input. Although the introduction says this file is selected through unit testing, the general selection procedure, failure handling, and localization accuracy are not established. Clarify what information is inferred versus supplied by the benchmark, and whether initial file-localization failures are included in the results.

Reproduction requires additional experimental details, including exact model snapshots, decoding settings, the agent resampling limit m, sampled bug identifiers, and retrieval configuration. Algorithm 1 also returns unconditionally inside its outer retry loop at line 54, making k ineffective as written. Reusing CoCoNuT training data does not itself establish that retrieval is disjoint from evaluation bugs. These validation and protocol gaps drive the resubmit-next-cycle assessment; resolving them is necessary for a sound Findings recommendation.
